notes: Complete Chancery trial judgment on penthouse roof-space lease forfeiture and consent to assign.

enrichment.short_title: Landlord unreasonably withheld consent to mortgagee's assignment of roof-space lease and waived forfeiture for development delay
key_facts: Two linked actions concerned a 1996 roof-space lease at Albert Court used for penthouse development, charged to First Penthouse Ltd (FP) and with the reversion held by CHAPS under an overriding lease.
FP assigned the lease to Mr Tamimi without CHAPS consent after CHAPS refused unless Tamimi assumed obligations under collateral Preliminary and Introduction Agreements benefiting Britel and Meretz.

CHAPS served section 146 notices for failure to complete development expeditiously and for unauthorised assignment; FP conceded breach of the development covenant but argued waiver and that consent had been unreasonably withheld.

CHAPS exercised an Option under the Preliminary Agreement and accepted £7 rent after the assignment, but the court held the development breach was a once-and-for-all breach and that CHAPS had irrevocably waived forfeiture.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Trial in the Chancery Division of consolidated actions for a declaration on consent to assign and on CHAPS's entitlement to forfeit the lease.
enrichment.outcome: Declaration that CHAPS unreasonably withheld consent to assignment; CHAPS held to have waived the right to forfeit for development delay; second action dismissed on those issues.
enrichment.ratio: A landlord may not refuse consent to an assignment on grounds collateral to the landlord-and-tenant relationship, including loss of personal contractual rights under related development agreements; where a 1999 Deed of Priorities authorised the mortgagee to override such rights, refusal on that basis was unreasonable; a once-and-for-all breach of a covenant to complete works expeditiously may be waived by equivocal acts of affirmation such as exercising a contractual option or accepting rent after the right to forfeit has arisen; covenants in collateral agreements for commission and development subleases were personal to the original lessee and not tenant covenants annexed under the 1995 Act.
legal_issues: Whether CHAPS waived forfeiture for failure to complete the Project expeditiously
Whether refusal of consent to assign was reasonable under the Landlord and Tenant Act 1988
Whether collateral Preliminary and Introduction Agreement obligations were enforceable tenant covenants under the 1995 Act
Whether the 1999 Deed of Priorities precluded CHAPS from objecting to assignment on grounds that it would defeat Britel's Option and Meretz's commission

enrichment.short_title: Judicial review of Hackney parking designation order barred by six-week ouster in Part VI of Schedule 9 to the Road Traffic Regulation Act 1984

statutes_considered.title: Local Authorities' Traffic Orders (Procedure) (England and Wales) Regulations 1996

key_facts: Claimants sought judicial review of a Hackney controlled parking zone designation order made on 20 January 2003 under section 45 of the Road Traffic Regulation Act 1984.
Proceedings were commenced on 10 April 2003, well outside the six-week period prescribed by Part VI of Schedule 9 for challenging designation orders.
Late in the hearing the defendant raised the ouster provision; the parties agreed to assume the order had been signed by an officer without proper delegated authority.

The claimants argued that absent valid authority the order was not a designation order within Part VI; the court held the challenge was still a challenge to validity on grounds of lack of relevant powers.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review hearing in the Administrative Court after permission was granted following refusal on the papers.
enrichment.outcome: Application for judicial review failed because Part VI of Schedule 9 barred challenge outside the six-week period.
enrichment.ratio: Part VI of Schedule 9 to the Road Traffic Regulation Act 1984 excludes judicial review of designation orders except by application to the High Court within six weeks on specified grounds; a challenge that the maker lacked authority to make the order is a challenge that the order was not within the relevant powers and must be brought within that statutory procedure, even where the order appears valid on its face.
legal_issues: Whether Part VI of Schedule 9 ousted jurisdiction where the order was made without proved delegated authority
Whether a challenge based on lack of authority fell within paragraph 35(a) as not within the relevant powers
Whether improper purpose and consultation defects could otherwise be pursued in judicial review

notes: Complete Court of Appeal judgment on fitness to plead directions and PACE s.78.

enrichment.short_title: Trial judge's Pritchard-based fitness-to-plead directions upheld where appellant with anterograde amnesia was found fit to stand trial
key_facts: The appellant was convicted of rape, indecent assault, indecency with a child and taking indecent photographs after a jury found him fit to plead.
Defence case at the fitness hearing was that anterograde amnesia from alcohol-related brain damage rendered him unable to follow proceedings, instruct lawyers or give evidence.

Psychiatric evidence was divided; the trial judge gave detailed written directions listing six capacities required for fitness and said failure on any one on the balance of probabilities would render the defendant unfit.
Police interview transcripts from 2001 were admitted at the fitness hearing over section 78 objection; the Court of Appeal upheld both the directions and that ruling.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against conviction by leave of the trial judge on the ground that fitness-to-plead directions may have set the threshold too low.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; application for leave to appeal on admissibility of interview transcripts refused.
enrichment.ratio: The Pritchard test remains the governing formulation for fitness to plead; a defendant need not remember the events giving rise to the charges and instructions need not be plausible or reliable; the judge's six-point directions faithfully applied that test and were not too low; fitness is ultimately for the jury on the evidence; admission of earlier police interviews at a fitness hearing is a matter for the trial judge's section 78 discretion absent perversity.
legal_issues: Whether the trial judge's fitness-to-plead directions set the legal threshold too low
Whether the jury's finding of fitness was perverse on the psychiatric evidence
Whether police interview transcripts from 2001 were admissible at the December 2002 fitness hearing

notes: Complete section 289 planning appeal judgment; appellants appeared in person.

enrichment.short_title: Planning appeal dismissed where Inspector lawfully refused change of use of garden annex to separate dwelling at Southwater
key_facts: Mr and Mrs Holding appealed under section 289 against an Inspector's dismissal of their appeal against refusal of planning permission to change use of Birchwood Lodge, a garden annex at Birchwood House, Southwater, to a separate dwelling.
The annex had been built under permitted development rights and lawfully used ancillary to the main house until the occupier's death.

The Inspector found no material considerations outweighing development plan policies and that a separate dwelling would adversely affect character and appearance, including because the appeal plot was significantly smaller than neighbouring plots.
Appellants argued procedural unfairness and lack of evidence for the plot-size finding; the court held the issue had been flagged by the council and was open on the plans and site view.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Statutory appeal under section 289 of the Town and Country Planning Act 1990 against a Planning Inspector's decision.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; defendants' costs assessed at £2,800.
enrichment.ratio: Change of use to a separate dwelling is 'development' within section 55(1); where section 54A required determination in accordance with the development plan and the Inspector found no material considerations sufficient to outweigh plan policies, the appeal failed irrespective of the character-and-appearance issue; an Inspector's site-based assessment of relative plot size was not irrational where the council had identified character impact and the appellants' own map was partly misleading.
legal_issues: Whether the Inspector misapplied local plan policies by treating change of use as 'development'
Whether there was procedural unfairness in relying on relative plot size without prior warning
Whether the plot-size finding was supported by evidence

notes: Full Lindsay J test-case judgment on teachers' ill-health retirement and Reg 7.

enrichment.short_title: Teachers who accepted ill-health retirement benefits had no public law right to compel employer dismissal under Regulation 7

statutes_considered.title: Education (Teachers' Qualifications and Health Standards) (England) Regulations 1999

key_facts: Three test cases involved teachers employed under the Burgundy Book who applied for and accepted ill-health retirement benefits (IHRB) on grounds of permanent incapacity but refused to resign and sought mandatory orders requiring dismissal.

Clause 6.1 of the Burgundy Book entitles a teacher given notice of termination for permanent incapacity to full salary for the notice period, but creates no contractual duty on the employer to serve such notice.
Teachers' Pensions guidance and Form 18 told applicants to arrange for employment to terminate at the earliest retirement date if IHRB was granted.
Over a hundred similar disputes were pending nationally on whether Regulation 7 of the 1999 Regulations imposed a public law duty on employers to dismiss.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review test cases in the Administrative Court seeking mandatory orders requiring local education authorities to dismiss teachers who had accepted IHRB.
enrichment.outcome: Claims dismissed; leave to appeal granted in each case.
enrichment.ratio: Where a teacher voluntarily applies for and accepts IHRB on permanent incapacity, employment is brought to an end by resignation or operation of law before any public law duty to dismiss could arise; Regulation 7 does not create a freestanding public law duty on employers to dismiss in such cases, and even if employment continued in a shadowy form it would not be 'relevant employment as a teacher' within the regulation.
legal_issues: Whether acceptance of IHRB terminated employment by resignation following Healey
Whether Regulation 7 automatically terminated employment by operation of law
Whether permanent incapacity frustrated the employment contract
Whether Regulation 7 imposed a public law duty on employers to dismiss teachers who had accepted IHRB

enrichment.short_title: Leaving stop notice at company's registered or principal office suffices for service under section 233 of the Local Government Act 1972
key_facts: Gloucestershire County Council prosecuted Keyway (Gloucester) Ltd for contravening a stop notice prohibiting importation and deposit of waste at Colemans Farm.
Justices dismissed the information on the preliminary ground that the stop notice had not been validly served on the company.
A process server left the notice at both the registered office and principal office with unidentified persons rather than handing it directly to the company secretary.
An enforcement notice had already been served; the stop notice was dated 13 November 2002 and was to take effect on 19 November 2002.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Prosecutor's appeal by way of case stated from magistrates' court to the High Court on validity of service of a stop notice.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; case remitted to justices to continue the hearing; respondent ordered to pay costs summarily assessed at £6,759.91.
enrichment.ratio: Under section 233 of the Local Government Act 1972, 'person' includes a body corporate and a stop notice may be served on a company by leaving it at its registered or principal office without proof of delivery into the hands of a director or secretary; section 233 methods are additional to section 329 of the Town and Country Planning Act 1990, which requires delivery to the secretary or clerk at the registered office or service by post.
legal_issues: Whether leaving a stop notice at a company's registered or principal office constitutes service under section 233
Whether service required delivery into the hands of a director or company secretary
Whether criminal liability for breach of a stop notice required stricter service rules

enrichment.short_title: Conviction appeal dismissed where read witness statements and summing-up challenges failed in rape and GBH trial
key_facts: Stacey Duncan was convicted of two counts of rape and one of inflicting grievous bodily harm after an incident following a West End nightclub visit in March 2002.
The complainant alleged coercion, vaginal and anal rape at the appellant's flat, then escaped through a bathroom window and fell two storeys, fracturing her arm.
Flatmate Johnny Hoyt did not attend trial; his two statements were read under section 23(2)(b) after the defence did not seek an adjournment.
The appellant's case was consensual sex; medical evidence showed anal laceration and injuries consistent with a fall but no strangulation signs.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against conviction by leave of the single judge following trial at Middlesex Guildhall Crown Court.
enrichment.ratio: The Pritchard-based fitness directions were not replicated here; instead the court held that read witness statements under section 23(2)(b) were properly admitted where the defence chose that course without adjournment; disparaging comments in a summing-up about the weight of unreadable witness evidence and character directions did not render the trial unfair; an early majority verdict direction did not make convictions unsafe where the jury returned further unanimous and majority verdicts after further deliberation.
legal_issues: Whether Johnny Hoyt's statements should have been read rather than calling him as a witness
Whether the judge unfairly diminished the weight of Hoyt's evidence in summing-up
Whether character and general summing-up comments were biased against the defence
Whether the majority verdict direction was given too soon

notes: Complete extradition habeas corpus judgment on delay and oppression under s.11(3)(b).

enrichment.short_title: Extradition to New Zealand for historic priest sex offences not unjust or oppressive despite 20-year average delay
key_facts: New Zealand sought extradition of Woodcock, a former Roman Catholic priest and UK resident, on 19 charges of indecent assault and one of buggery involving 11 male complainants, mostly from 1982-1985.
He was committed after a prima facie case was found at Bow Street in February 2003 following arrest in August 2002.
Initial complaints were made in 1994-1995 but no extradition request followed; further complainants came forward after a 2002 television programme.
Woodcock argued return would be unjust because a fair trial was impossible and oppressive because he had built a new life in England since leaving New Zealand in 1987.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Habeas corpus application under section 11(3)(b) of the Extradition Act 1989 following committal for extradition.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; no order as to costs.
enrichment.ratio: Section 11(3)(b) requires the court to ask whether return would be unjust or oppressive in all the circumstances; 'unjust' primarily concerns risk of prejudice at trial and 'oppressive' concerns hardship from changed circumstances, but the court may have regard to safeguards in the requesting state's law; where New Zealand courts can stay prosecutions for abuse of process and multiple complainants with supporting evidence make a fair trial possible, long delay alone does not bar extradition; building a new life abroad after leaving freely does not ordinarily make return oppressive for grave offences.
legal_issues: Whether passage of time made trial unjust under section 11(3)(b)
Whether changed circumstances in England made return oppressive
Whether the court should defer to New Zealand abuse-of-process jurisdiction
Whether cluster of complaints following a television programme affected fairness

notes: Complete appeal on recent complaint re-examination and sentence reduction.

enrichment.short_title: Judge erred allowing re-examination on recent complaint but convictions safe; indecent assault sentences reduced to 18 months
key_facts: Ali was convicted of three indecent assaults on an 11-year-old girl, T, and one on her mother, P, in shared local authority accommodation.
The Crown did not rely on T's complaint to P as recent complaint evidence because of inconsistencies, but defence cross-examination exposed inconsistencies in locations and frequency.
The judge allowed prosecution re-examination of P to add consistent details of T's complaint, relying on R v Riley and rejecting R v Beattie.
Ali was sentenced to three years' imprisonment with a deportation recommendation; the court reduced total sentence to 18 months.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against conviction and sentence by leave of the single judge in the Court of Appeal (Criminal Division).
enrichment.outcome: Conviction appeal dismissed; sentence appeal allowed in part with total sentence reduced from three years to 18 months.
enrichment.ratio: There is no general fourth exception to the rule against previous consistent statements permitting re-examination to show consistency after cross-examination on inconsistency; Riley and section 5 of the 1865 Act do not create such an exception outside recognised categories in Beattie; nevertheless convictions may remain safe where the judge directed that the complaint was not evidence of truth and the jury separately convicted on the mother's account; sentences for these indecent assaults were manifestly excessive compared with guideline authorities.
legal_issues: Whether the judge wrongly permitted re-examination to prove consistency in T's recent complaint
Whether the evidential error rendered convictions on counts relating to T unsafe
Whether three years' imprisonment was manifestly excessive

notes: Complete Companies Court judgment staying LLP winding-up petition pending arbitration.

enrichment.short_title: Winding-up petition against investment-advice LLP stayed pending arbitration of partners' misconduct allegations
key_facts: Magi Capital Partners LLP was formed in August 2002 by four partners to provide FSA-regulated investment advice until a major investor withdrew in June 2003.

Two partners petitioned to wind up the LLP on the just and equitable ground after deadlock and breakdown; the third partner, Banerjee, applied to stay the petition pending arbitration under the partnership agreement.
Banerjee alleged the petitioners changed locks and passwords and sought his expulsion on spurious grounds; the parties had agreed an arbitrator but petitioners then issued the winding-up petition.
The partnership agreement contained a broad arbitration clause covering disputes relating to the firm and partner conduct.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application in the Companies Court to stay or adjourn a just-and-equitable winding-up petition pending arbitration.
enrichment.outcome: Petition stayed until 19 January with case management conference thereafter; costs reserved to the judge hearing the petition.
enrichment.ratio: Although an LLP may be wound up under section 122(1)(g) of the Insolvency Act 1986 and statutory winding-up cannot be contractually excluded, a stay is appropriate where allegations material to whether winding up is just and equitable are within a binding arbitration clause and are better determined by the arbitrator first; conduct of petitioners alleged to have caused breakdown may be relevant under authorities such as Ebrahimi and Vujnovich even where trading has ceased.
legal_issues: Whether a winding-up petition could be stayed in favour of contractual arbitration in an LLP
Whether Banerjee's misconduct allegations were material to the just-and-equitable ground
Whether the petition was an abuse to frustrate arbitration
Appropriate duration and costs of the stay
